sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Three contracting approaches for permanent anchored systems: method, performance (end result) and contractor design/build; the owner should never specify anchor installation details and all should use performance-based anchor acceptance. Owners should adopt a formal policy on design and contracting.
sections.body: The chapter describes contracting approaches for permanent anchored systems: (1) method, (2) performance, (3) contractor design/build, with differing owner and contractor responsibility for design, construction and performance; long experience shows the owner should not specify anchor installation details, and all approaches should use performance based acceptance criteria for anchors (see also Nicholson and Bruce, 1992; Deaton, 1994; FHWA-DP-96-69R, 1998; FHWA-RD-97-130, 1998). Method approach: method specifications for owner or material-supplier designs, materials and execution specified explicitly except anchor type and installation details (section 8.2). Performance approach: an end result specification using approved or generic systems, with lines, grades and geometric, design and performance criteria, the contractor submitting project-specific calculations and plans with working drawings (section 8.3). Contractor design/build: like performance but with design, construction and performance solely the specialty contractor's, requiring strict prequalification and performance-based submittals at key times (section 8.4). Each works if properly implemented; choice depends on owner and consultant experience, project complexity, availability of specialty contractors or suppliers and agency philosophy. Each owner should develop a formal policy (p. 157) to: obtain agency uniformity in selecting anchored and other retaining systems; set procedures for technical review and acceptance of proprietary and generic systems; assign internal responsibility for accepting new systems, plan preparation, design review and construction control; develop uniform design and performance criteria and construction and material specifications; and set guidelines for choosing method, performance or design/build approaches. (pp. 156 to 157)
key_points: Method, performance and contractor design/build approaches (p. 156).
Owner should not specify anchor installation details (p. 156).
Performance-based anchor acceptance in all approaches (p. 156).
Choice by experience, complexity, contractor availability, agency philosophy (p. 156).
Owners should adopt a formal anchored system policy (p. 157).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Method contracts give detailed plans and specifications but leave anchor selection and installation to the contractor, setting only minimum hole diameter, unbonded and bond lengths; suited to experienced owners, who bear design and performance responsibility and pay for changes.
sections.body: The method approach develops a detailed set of plans and material and construction specifications for bidding, but anchor selection and installation are the contractor's: the documents set only minimum drill hole diameter, unbonded length and bond length, and the contractor chooses dimensions and techniques to pass the acceptance tests; in no case should the owner specify anchor installation details. Advantages: complete design and specifications developed and reviewed over an extended period, letting owner engineers examine options, but requiring staff trained in all areas of earth retaining technology; best where the owner has significant anchored wall experience. Disadvantages: alternate bids mean more designs to review though one wall is built; agency staff may overlook newer, more cost-effective systems and unfamiliar proprietary equipment and methods. Under a method approach the owner and inspector are fully responsible for design and performance if the contractor built to the specifications, and the owner must direct and pay for changes. (p. 157)
key_points: Only minimum hole diameter, unbonded and bond lengths specified (p. 157).
Owner never specifies anchor installation details (p. 157).
Best for experienced owners (p. 157).
Owner responsible for design and performance; pays for changes (p. 157).

sections.title: Contract Documents for Method Approach
sections.summary: Method contract documents are drawings, specifications and bid items (lump sum or unit price): alignment, elevations, cross sections, notes and constraints, typical sections, tolerances, connection details, payment limits, plus wall elements, lagging and facing, anchor locations and connections, corrosion protection, anchor capacity and lengths, and testing and lock-off requirements.
sections.body: Method contract documents comprise drawings, specifications and bid items and quantities, bid lump sum or by detailed unit prices. Drawings typically include at least: horizontal alignment by stations and offsets to the wall face and appurtenances; top and bottom elevations, beginning and end stations, positions along the wall and final ground line; cross sections with construction limits, underground interferences (utilities, piles of adjacent structures), backfill, excavation limits and mean high, design high and drawdown water levels as applicable; construction notes and constraints (staging, vertical clearance, right-of-way, easements, noise and air quality); typical sections and special details; construction tolerances; connections to traffic barriers, copings, parapets, noise walls and lighting; payment limits and quantities. Anchored wall items: size, type, location, installation method and minimum embedment of all wall elements; timber lagging thickness and facing details and connections to soldier piles, sheet-piles and/or walers; locations of all anchors and their connection details; corrosion protection for anchorage, unbonded length and bond length; required anchor capacity, inclination, minimum unbonded length and minimum bond length for each anchor (p. 159); and methods and frequency of proof, performance, extended creep and lift-off testing, acceptance criteria and required lock-off load. (pp. 158 to 159)
key_points: Drawings, specifications, bid items; lump sum or unit price (p. 158).
General drawing contents: alignment, elevations, sections, constraints, tolerances (p. 158).
Anchor items: capacity, inclination, minimum unbonded and bond lengths (pp. 158 to 159).
Testing methods and frequency, acceptance criteria, lock-off load (p. 159).

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: In performance contracts the owner sets scope, geometry, loads, materials, performance and monitoring and the contractor designs, cutting owner engineering cost; owner staff may lack expertise to review designs. Methods: pre-bid wall design, pre-bid typical section design and post-bid design.
sections.body: The owner establishes the scope and prepares drawings of geometric requirements, design loadings, allowed materials or components, performance requirements and instrumentation or monitoring requirements. With proper specifications and prequalification of suppliers, specialty contractors and materials, the approach offers benefits: design by a trained and experienced contractor or consultant, lower owner engineering cost and manpower, and design cost shifted to construction. Its disadvantage is that owner engineers may be inexperienced with anchored systems and not fully qualified to review designs and modifications, possibly rejecting newer cost-effective methods. Three methods implement it, pre-bid wall design, pre-bid typical section design and post-bid design, differing in when design is done; two-phase bidding and negotiated proposals have been used on special projects (Nicholson and Bruce, 1992). (p. 159)
key_points: Owner sets geometry, loads, materials, performance, monitoring (p. 159).
Contractor designs; owner engineering cost reduced (p. 159).
Owner review expertise may be lacking (p. 159).
Pre-bid wall, pre-bid typical section, post-bid design (p. 159).

sections.title: Pre-bid Wall Design
sections.summary: Pre-bid wall design: specialty contractors prepare detailed designs before advertisement from owner data, and approved designs go into the bid documents with an owner generic design; only experienced contractors are likely to submit.
sections.body: Contract documents allow various wall alternates: the owner tells specialty contractors a wall is proposed and asks for detailed designs before bid advertisement, based on owner line and grade, geotechnical and subsurface information and design requirements; approved designs are included in the bid documents, letting the owner review details from several contractors. Given the detail required, only contractors with significant anchored system expertise are likely to submit (p. 160). The owner should also include a generic wall design so general contractors can choose it or a specialty contractor's design. (pp. 159 to 160)
key_points: Detailed contractor designs before advertisement (p. 159).
Approved designs included in bid documents (p. 159).
Owner includes a generic design too (p. 160).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects

sections.title: Pre-bid Typical Section Design
sections.summary: Pre-bid typical section design: prequalified contractors submit schematic plans to owner requirements, more likely to participate with little effort, but loosely defined requirements can cause misunderstandings and claims (e.g., facing concrete from soldier beam tolerances, Deaton 1994).
sections.body: Prequalified specialty contractors develop schematic or conceptual plans to the owner's geometric and performance requirements, with enough detail for the owner to judge acceptability; contractors typically omit details unique to their design. Compared with pre-bid wall design, specialty contractors are more likely to submit, needing little effort, with detailed design and working drawings only if successful. The disadvantage is less well defined requirements, which may lead to misunderstandings and claims; where the general contractor does not build the anchored system, the lack of detail may cause problems, e.g., approved soldier beam tolerances requiring more facing concrete than anticipated (Deaton, 1994). (p. 160)
key_points: Schematic plans from prequalified contractors (p. 160).
More contractor participation, little preparation effort (p. 160).
Less defined requirements risk claims (Deaton 1994) (p. 160).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects

sections.title: Post-bid Wall Design
sections.summary: Post-bid wall design: bid documents name walls and acceptable alternates; general contractors carry a specialty contractor's design and price, with detailed calculations and working drawings for owner approval after award; the owner gains experience but less control.
sections.body: The post-bid approach also allows prequalified contractor-designed alternates. Bid documents identify each wall and acceptable alternates, with design requirements in special provisions or standard specifications. General contractors take bids from prequalified specialty contractors and include a selected design and price; after award, if the general contractor builds the anchored system, the specialty contractor prepares detailed calculations and working drawings for owner review and approval, and the walls are built to them. The owner benefits from contractor or supplier experience but has less control than with pre-bid approval of working drawings, and a risk-averse general contractor will likely not choose an alternate unless savings are significant. (p. 160)
key_points: Walls and alternates identified in bid documents (p. 160).
Detailed design and working drawings after award for approval (p. 160).
Less owner control than pre-bid approval (p. 160).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects

sections.title: Contract Documents for Performance Approach
sections.summary: Performance contract documents must give geometric and site data, design guidelines (agency manuals or AASHTO, loads, drainage, seismic, minimum factors of safety, geotechnical parameters, facing) and performance requirements (design life, corrosion protection, anchor testing and acceptance, tolerable movements, groundwater limits), plus monitoring.
sections.body: Whatever the performance method, the owner includes geometric and site data, design guidelines and performance requirements, usually with an instrumentation and monitoring program covering performance, proof and extended creep tests, minimum instrumentation and threshold values. Geometric and Site Data: horizontal alignment; top and bottom elevations, stations, positions and final ground line; cross sections with construction limits, backfill, excavation limits and water levels; construction constraints (staging, clearance, right-of-way, easements); utilities, signs and their loads; subsurface investigation and testing data. Design Guidelines: governing sections of agency design manuals (materials, structural, hydraulic, geotechnical), construction specifications and special provisions, or current AASHTO Standard Specifications if none; magnitude, location and direction of external loads from bridges, overhead signs and lights and traffic surcharges; drainage features beneath, behind, above or through the structure; seismic requirements; minimum factors of safety for overall stability, anchor pullout, tendon rupture, axial and lateral wall capacity, etc.; geotechnical parameters (friction angle, cohesion, unit weight) and electrochemical properties (p. 162); type, size and architectural treatment of facing. Performance Requirements: design life and corrosion protection; anchor testing and acceptance criteria; tolerable horizontal and vertical movements and their measurement where movement sensitive structures exist behind the wall, movement control being considered for structures within a horizontal distance of one-half the wall height from the top; permissible groundwater variation and its measurement, groundwater control being considered near existing structures. (pp. 161 to 162)
key_points: Geometric and site data, design guidelines, performance requirements (p. 161).
Monitoring program with test requirements and thresholds (p. 161).
Minimum factors of safety for each failure mechanism (p. 161).
Movement control for structures within H/2 of the wall top (p. 162).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects

sections.title: Review and Approval
sections.summary: Agency structural and geotechnical engineers must review performance designs rigorously, before or after bid: line and grade, conformance to standards (e.g., AASHTO), corrosion protection, details at obstructions, drainage, facing, monitoring and anchor field testing.
sections.body: Review may come before or after the bid depending on the method. Evaluation by agency structural and geotechnical engineers must be rigorous and consider at least: conformance to line and grade; conformance of calculations to agency standards, special provisions or codes such as current AASHTO Standard Specifications; corrosion protection details; design details at obstructions such as drainage structures; external and internal drainage; architectural treatment of the face; monitoring methods required by the specifications; and field testing program details for anchor capacity. (p. 162)
key_points: Rigorous agency review before or after bid (p. 162).
Eight minimum review items, from line and grade to anchor testing (p. 162).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects

sections.title: Contractor Design/Build Approach
sections.summary: In contractor design/build the owner sets requirements, supplies subsurface data and provides quality assurance; the specialty contractor is responsible for design, construction and performance, pre-bid or post-bid; most used for temporary anchors.
sections.body: In the other approaches owner and contractor share responsibility. With contractor design/build, the owner outlines requirements, obtains complete subsurface and geotechnical information and provides construction quality assurance, and the specialty contractor is responsible for complete design, construction and performance. Proposals may come before advertisement (pre-bid) or after award (post-bid). It is most often used for temporary anchor projects but has been used for permanent walls; success depends on communicating basic design concepts to the owner and jointly developing a quality assurance plan before construction. (p. 163)
key_points: Specialty contractor responsible for design, construction, performance (p. 163).
Owner supplies requirements, subsurface data, quality assurance (p. 163).
Mostly temporary anchor projects (p. 163).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.summary: Whatever the approach, anchor construction details should be performance based and solely the contractor's; the owner specifies minimums (corrosion protection, unbonded and bond lengths, inclination, total length from right-of-way, acceptance criteria). Prequalify specialty contractors on similar ground and region.
sections.body: All three approaches have been used for anchor work. Regardless of approach, a performance based approach should be used for anchor construction details: specialty contractors have developed systems, equipment and methods for specific conditions and must stay current competitively, so agencies benefit by specifying anchor performance rather than components. The owner must specify minimum requirements: corrosion protection for anchors and other components, minimum unbonded and bond length, inclination and total anchor length from right-of-way restrictions, and acceptance/rejection criteria; construction details should be solely the contractor's responsibility. Prequalification of specialty contractors is essential, based on successful design and construction experience in similar ground and in the region of the project. (p. 163)
key_points: Performance based anchor construction details in every approach (p. 163).
Owner minimums: corrosion protection, lengths, inclination, acceptance criteria (p. 163).
Construction details solely the contractor's (p. 163).
Prequalify on similar ground and region (p. 163).
sections.applicability: Contract document preparation and responsibility allocation for anchored wall projects
